analytic.title: An Adaptive Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization for Mapping Real-Time Applications onto Network-on-a-Chip based MPSoCs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents a modified version of the well-known Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm as an alternative for the single-objective Genetic Algorithm (GA) that is currently the state-of-the-art method to map real-time applications tasks onto Multiple Processors System-on-a-Chip (MPSoC) using preemptive capable wormhole-based Network-on-a-Chip (NoC) as their communication architecture. A statistical study based on an experimental setup has been performed to compare the GA-based task mapper and the proposed method by using a real-time application as a benchmark, as well as a group of randomly generated ones. Preliminary results have shown that our method is capable of achieving quicker convergence than the GA-based method, and it even produces better results when the application utilization is smaller than the available processing capacity, i.e., a fully schedulable mapping solution exists.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-Time Systems (RTS) represent an essential part of modern computing infrastructure, being mandatory to comply with the correctness of the results yielded by the algorithms as well as to fulfill the time restrictions related to the dynamics of physical processes. The number of applications related to RTS has been growing in recent years, by including interconnected computing resources and involving applications widespread in vital areas such as critical embedded devices developed for automotive and aerospace industries. As we approach the end of Moore's law, these devices meet their goals of performance growth by relying on heavy parallelism using many processing cores in the same die as Multiple Processor System-on-a-Chip (MPSoC) solutions [18]. In this context, Network-on-a-Chip (NoC) [4] is an acknowledged communication paradigm for MPSoCs embedded devices consisting of an interconnected fabric that allows data exchange between processing cores using routers and links in each tile.

Real-Time Networks-on-a-Chip (RTNoC) [7] are NoCs that offer architectural support for constraints imposed by RTS in which their performance depends on the logical correctness as well as their time-bounded responses for their application tasks and intra-chip communication latencies. Examples of RTNoC designs [2] [13] holds the following features: (a) wormhole switching strategy that decreases the necessary sizes in routers' buffers by dividing the messages into smaller transmission units called flits and sending these flits in a pipeline manner through the network; (b) 2D meshgrid topology due to its simplicity; (c) a deterministic and predictable routing algorithm such as an XY-routing algorithm; also, (d) routers with virtual channels [3] mechanism that increases the NoC throughput as well as the predictability SBCCI '19, August 26-30, 2019, Sao Paulo, Brazil Barros, et al.
of messages transmissions by allowing message preemption based on their priority levels.

Due to the broad range of design possibilities in a NoCbased system allied with the time constraints inherent from RTS, it is imperative for the design of an MPSoC (with RT-NoC) to consider the characteristics of the Real-Time Application (RTA) since the early stages of the project. Mapping RTA in MPSoCs can be faced by defining an analytic method to quickly evaluate each mapping, such as the End-to-End Response Time (EERT) analysis [8]. This strategy allows the designer for a broader range of possible task placements that can be evaluated by addressing the problem as an optimization Task Mapping Problem (TMP). This approach can also be used on both hard and soft real-time settings, depending upon the tolerated number of unschedulable tasks.

TMP is an NP-hard problem in which the mapping of an application with n tasks onto a system with m cores reflects in a search space with m n possible mappings [12] making a bruteforce approach computationally unfeasible. For this reason, the use of soft-computing search algorithms is welcomed for this problem, and previous related works have demonstrated that Genetic Algorithm (GA) based approaches are capable of achieving fully schedulable task mapping placements for MPSoCs, based on wormhole-based NoC [14] [15].

In this work, we present an alternative metaheuristic based on the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm, called Adaptive Discrete PSO with Utilization factor (ADPSO-U), that contains a local-search method that uses the information about the problem to achieve full-schedulable solutions with faster convergence. The experimental setup uses a RTA benchmark as well as synthetically generated applications, and the obtained results show that the ASPSO-U is competitive against GA-based mappers for scenarios where platforms have enough processing capability to have at least a feasible fully schedulable mapping placement.

div.head: TASK MAPPING AS AN OPTIMIZATION PROBLEM
div.p: In this work, the analytic end-to-end schedulability test [8] is used along with its application and platform models to evaluate the quality of RTA task mappings onto the system. It permits a quick assessment of whether the tasks' end-to-end response time (EERT) is smaller than their relative deadline during the critical instant, the worst possible scenario in which all tasks are released at the same time and compete for system resources. For each task, the EERT is composed of the sum of tasks worst-case response time (WCRT) and their emitted messages worst-case network latency (WCL), if there are any.

div.p: The platform model Ψ represents a RTNoC based MPSoC composed of a set of homogeneous processors and their network interface (NI) Π = {π 1 , π 2 , ..., π n }. Π is connected to a set of routers R = {ρ 1 , ρ 2 , ..., ρ n } that are also connected between them via a set of unidirectional links

The RTA model represented as Ω that has a set of tasks Γ and a set of packetized messages Φ. Each task is a tuple τ = C,T , D, J , R, P, ϕ formed, respectively, by the worstcase execution time (WCET), inter-arrival period, relative deadline time, release jitter that equals 0, WCRT, prioritylevel, and a message ϕ sent after the task execution to another task in Ω. Each message ϕ ∈ Φ, namely a flow of flits, is in turn represented by a tuple ϕ = τ d , L, Z , K, S , where τ d is the destination task, L is the basic network latency, i.e., the message latency when there is no network contention, Z is the flow size in flits, K is the maximum release jitter for that message that is equal to its source task WCRT, and S is the message WCL. In this model, the following assumptions are made for the analysis: (a) tasks deadlines are equal to their periods D = T ; (b) tasks transmit a single flow at the end of their executions; (c) each processor π has a processing queue ordered by priority permitting tasks preemption; and (e) each message inherits the priority from its source task.

div.head: PROPOSED ADAPTIVE DISCRETE PARTICLE SWARM OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHM (ADPSO-U)
div.p: ADPSO-U is a modified version of the Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm (DPSO) proposed in [9] containing an adaptive parameter control mechanism that enables the algorithm to adjust its parameters while solving the problem, by eliminating the necessity of a fine-tuning process for the algorithm as defined in [6]. Algorithm 2 displays ADPSO-U in pseudo-code form. ADPSO-U contains a swarm P of N particles and each ith particle during iteration k has a position x (k) i , velocity v (k ) i , best individual and global positions x i,pbest and x дbest , akin to the canonical PSO [10]. Each particle's position is a |Γ|-dimensional integer vector and each of its components vary between [0, |Π|). Position x i of particle i represents a possible task mapping summed up element-by-element by one, i.e. x i = M i + 1 with 1 being a |Γ|-dimension vector of ones.
ADPSO-U uses Eqs. ( 6) and ( 7) to update each ith particle velocity and position, respectively.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS
div.p: The experimental setup uses task mappers based on our proposed algorithm ADPSO-U and a single-objective genetic algorithm (GA) to optimize a set of 10 task mapping problems using multiple RTA and platforms with different sizes to perform a preliminary evaluation of ADPSO-U against GA.

The work in [15] describes the GA used and also presents a fine-tuning process to identify the best parameters for GA for the task mapping problem. The obtained parameters were crossover rate of p c = 0.8 and mutation probability of p m = 0.01. Since ADPSO-U has an adaptive parameter control mechanism, a similar tuning process is unnecessary.

The used platforms have mesh-grid sizes of 3x4, 4x4, and 4x5, containing, respectively, 12, 16, and 20 homogeneous processors. These platforms have the following characteristics: (a) clock of 50 MHz; (b) link width of 32 bits; (c) link and router latencies to emit a flit of 1 cycle and 10 cycles.

The set of applications used has a default RTA benchmark used in previous related works (AVA [8]) as well as synthetic RTAs, namely (TB1-5), that uses different random distributions to generate their utilization factors between 5% and 70%, respectively, Uniform, Exponential, Normal, Cauchy, and χ 2 distributions.

Table 1 presents information about each task mapping problem introducing the platform and application used where Ψ is the platform mesh-grid size, Zpayload is the median size of messages payloads in (KB) and U total is the application total utilization in (%). Both algorithms were configured to evaluate 2500 task mappings with number of search agents equal to 50 and both running for 50 iterations. For statistical analysis purposes, 32 experiments were executed to compare both algorithms, and the medians of their results were used for a Wilcoxon rank-sum non-parametric test, as suggested in [5]. Figure 3 shows in a box-plot format the distribution of results for both algorithms multiple executions for the problems used.

For the convergence analysis, we took only the task mapping TMP1, and its result is present in Figure 4. It is possible to observe that, in this case, our proposed algorithm was capable of obtaining task mappings with less unschedulable tasks in fewer iterations than the GA algorithm.

For the Wilcoxon rank-sum test [5], we analyze whether both algorithms results (our samples) were obtained from the same statistical population, our null hypothesis. This analysis is made by calculating the sum of ranks of task mapping problems that ADPSO-U outperforms GA for their median results (R + = 40) and the sum of ranks that the opposite happens (R -= 5) and, afterward comparing these rank-sum results with the Wilcoxon distribution table obtaining a pvalue of 0.039. In other words, the calculated p-value means that within a significance level of α = 5%, our proposed alternative algorithm obtained statistically better results in our experimental setup than the GA algorithm, by rejecting the null hypothesis.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents an Adaptive Discrete Particle Swarm Optimization with Utilization factor (ADPSO-U) capable of obtaining competitive results with fewer iterations when searching for schedulable task allocation solutions when mapping real-time applications (RTA) onto network-on-achip based MPSoCs with multiple homogeneous processors.

We also provide an experimental setup and a statistical analysis using a Wilcoxon non-parametric test to compare the results of our proposed algorithm against those of a single-objective GA based mapper, as used by previous related works [8] [15], with both methods performing end-toend schedulability analysis [8] to minimize the number of unschedulable tasks. The statistical analysis shows evidence that ADPSO-U could be used as an alternative for the GA when mapping RTA onto platforms capable of coping with the necessary processing resources to run these RTA.

In future works, we intend to extend our experimental analysis to compare the proposed algorithm in task mapping conditions with larger applications being mapped onto platforms with hundreds of processing cores.
